key_points: Occurs in the cytosol and does not require oxygen.
Splits one 6-carbon glucose into two 3-carbon pyruvates.
Yields a net of 2 ATP and 2 NADH.
Regulated by the enzyme phosphofructokinase, which is inhibited by ATP and activated by AMP.
concepts.source_ref: Lecture 12: Cellular respiration · Stage 1: Glycolysis

concepts.topic: Pyruvate Oxidation and the Citric Acid Cycle
key_points: Occurs in the mitochondrial matrix.
Pyruvate is converted to acetyl-CoA, releasing CO2 and making NADH.
Each turn of the cycle produces 3 NADH, 1 FADH2, and 1 ATP (or GTP).
The cycle turns twice for every glucose molecule.
concepts.source_ref: Lecture 12: Cellular respiration · Stage 2: Pyruvate oxidation and the citric acid cycle

key_points: Occurs in the inner mitochondrial membrane.
The electron transport chain pumps protons into the intermembrane space to build a gradient.
Oxygen acts as the final electron acceptor to form water.
ATP synthase uses the flow of protons back into the matrix to make ATP through chemiosmosis.
concepts.source_ref: Lecture 12: Cellular respiration · Stage 3: Oxidative phosphorylation

key_points: Occurs when oxygen is absent to regenerate NAD+ so glycolysis can continue.
Lactic acid fermentation reduces pyruvate to lactate.
Alcohol fermentation converts pyruvate to ethanol and CO2.
Yields only the 2 ATP produced during glycolysis.
concepts.source_ref: Lecture 12: Cellular respiration · Without oxygen: fermentation

key_points: Occur in the thylakoid membranes where chlorophyll absorbs blue and red light while reflecting green.
Photosystem II splits water to produce oxygen and sends excited electrons down an electron transport chain.
ATP is generated via a proton gradient and ATP synthase, while Photosystem I re-energizes electrons to produce NADPH.
concepts.source_ref: Lecture 15: Photosynthesis · Light reactions

key_points: Occurs in the stroma and consists of three phases: carbon fixation, reduction, and regeneration of RuBP.
The enzyme rubisco fixes CO2 by attaching it to RuBP, a 5-carbon sugar.
Uses ATP and NADPH from the light reactions to produce G3P, requiring 3 turns of the cycle per G3P and 2 G3P to make one glucose.
concepts.source_ref: Lecture 15: Photosynthesis · Calvin cycle

key_points: Happens when the enzyme rubisco binds O2 instead of CO2, which wastes energy and releases CO2.
Increases on hot, dry days when plants close their stomata to conserve water, causing internal CO2 levels to drop.
concepts.source_ref: Lecture 15: Photosynthesis · Photorespiration

key_points: C4 plants use PEP carboxylase to fix CO2 into a 4-carbon compound in mesophyll cells, then release it near rubisco in bundle-sheath cells.
CAM plants open their stomata at night to store CO2 as an acid, then run the Calvin cycle during the day with closed stomata.
Both pathways serve as adaptations to minimize photorespiration and conserve water in hot climates.
concepts.source_ref: Lecture 15: Photosynthesis · Adaptations

key_points: Interphase takes up about 90% of the cell cycle and consists of G1, S, and G2 phases.
During the S phase, DNA synthesis occurs, copying each chromosome into two sister chromatids joined at the centromere.
The M phase consists of mitosis and cytokinesis, while cells that stop dividing enter G0.
concepts.source_ref: Lecture 18: The cell cycle and mitosis · The cell cycle has two main parts

key_points: Mitosis progresses through prophase, prometaphase, metaphase, anaphase, and telophase (PMAT).
During anaphase, sister chromatids are separated and pulled to opposite poles as full chromosomes.
Cytokinesis divides the cytoplasm, forming a cleavage furrow in animal cells and a cell plate in plant cells.
The final product of mitosis is two genetically identical diploid cells.
concepts.source_ref: Lecture 18: The cell cycle and mitosis · Mitosis in order

key_points: Checkpoints (G1, G2, and M) decide whether the cell cycle proceeds based on size, DNA damage, and spindle attachment.
Cyclins are regulatory proteins whose levels fluctuate to activate cyclin-dependent kinases (CDKs).
MPF (maturation-promoting factor) is a specific cyclin-CDK complex that triggers entry into mitosis.
concepts.source_ref: Lecture 18: The cell cycle and mitosis · Control system

key_points: Cancer cells ignore checkpoint signals, lack density-dependent inhibition, and divide indefinitely.
p53 is a tumor suppressor gene that halts the cycle when DNA is damaged, and is mutated in about half of human cancers.
Proto-oncogenes normally promote division, but mutate into oncogenes that drive uncontrolled cell division.
concepts.source_ref: Lecture 18: The cell cycle and mitosis · Cancer

key_points: Catalase from potato extract breaks hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen.
The chemical reaction is represented as 2 H2O2 -> 2 H2O + O2.
The reaction rate is measured by the height of the oxygen foam in a graduated tube after 60 seconds.
concepts.source_ref: Lab 4 handout: Enzyme kinetics · Purpose

key_points: Part A of the lab tests five different concentrations of hydrogen peroxide from 0.5% to 8%.
The reaction rate rises with substrate concentration and then levels off.
At high concentrations, every enzyme molecule is busy, leading to saturation (Vmax) where adding more substrate does not speed up the reaction.
concepts.source_ref: Lab 4 handout: Enzyme kinetics · What you should see

key_points: Part B tests the reaction rate at 4 C, 22 C, 37 C, and 70 C using boiled extract.
The reaction rate rises with temperature up to an optimum near 37 C and collapses at 70 C.
At 70 C, heat breaks the weak bonds holding the active-site shape, causing the enzyme to denature.
Boiled extract still contains the enzyme, but the enzyme is denatured rather than absent.
concepts.source_ref: Lab 4 handout: Enzyme kinetics · What you should see / Common deductions

key_points: Water exhibits key properties including cohesion, high specific heat, and acting as a solvent.
These unique properties are explained by hydrogen bonds.
This topic is studied alongside pH, buffers, and the four classes of macromolecules.
concepts.source_ref: Midterm study guide (chapters 1–7) · Chapter 1-2

key_points: Passive transport includes diffusion, osmosis, and facilitated diffusion.
Active transport is distinguished from passive transport.
Cells behave differently depending on whether they are in hypotonic, isotonic, or hypertonic solutions.
concepts.source_ref: Midterm study guide (chapters 1–7) · Chapter 3-4

key_points: It is divided into glycolysis, the citric acid cycle, and oxidative phosphorylation.
Each stage must be understood by its location, inputs, outputs, and ATP yield.
It involves the roles of NADH and FADH2, chemiosmosis, and fermentation.
concepts.source_ref: Midterm study guide (chapters 1–7) · Chapter 6

key_points: It involves comparing light reactions and the Calvin cycle by location, inputs, and outputs.
Key components include photosystems II and I, and the enzyme rubisco.
Plants can use C4 and CAM adaptations to deal with photorespiration.
concepts.source_ref: Midterm study guide (chapters 1–7) · Chapter 7

key_points: Boyle's law states that pressure times volume is constant at fixed temperature and moles.
Charles's law states that volume divided by temperature is constant when temperature is in kelvin.
Avogadro's law states that volume divided by moles is constant.
Always convert Celsius to kelvin by adding 273.15.
concepts.source_ref: Chapter 5: Gases · Simple gas laws

key_points: The law is written as P V = n R T using the gas constant R = 0.08206 L atm / (mol K).
Standard temperature and pressure (STP) is 0 C and 1 atm, where one mole occupies 22.4 L.
It can be rearranged to calculate density as P M / (R T).
It can be rearranged to find molar mass as d R T / P.
concepts.source_ref: Chapter 5: Gases · Ideal gas law

key_points: Dalton's law states that the total pressure is the sum of the partial pressures.
The partial pressure of a gas equals its mole fraction multiplied by the total pressure.
For a gas collected over water, subtract the vapor pressure of water to determine the dry gas pressure.
concepts.source_ref: Chapter 5: Gases · Partial pressures

key_points: Gas particles move randomly, undergo elastic collisions, and have negligible volume compared to empty space.
Average kinetic energy of gas particles is proportional to kelvin temperature.
Lighter gases move faster than heavier gases at the same temperature.
Real gases deviate from ideal behavior under conditions of high pressure and low temperature.
concepts.source_ref: Chapter 5: Gases · Kinetic molecular theory

key_points: Use super to access superclass members.
Override methods from parent classes.
Understand dynamic dispatch.
Work with abstract classes, equals, and hashCode.
concepts.source_ref: Exam 1 topics list · Topics

key_points: Write tests and use assertions.
Use assertThrows for exception testing.
Understand test coverage.
concepts.source_ref: Exam 1 topics list · Topics

key_points: Distinguish between checked and unchecked exceptions.
Use try, catch, and finally blocks.
Create custom exceptions.
concepts.source_ref: Exam 1 topics list · Topics

concepts.topic: Finite state machines and the State pattern
key_points: Understand finite state machines.
Implement the State pattern.
Write state transitions from memory.
concepts.source_ref: Exam 1 topics list · Topics

key_points: The object's actual class decides which method runs, not the variable's declared type.
The declared type decides which methods you are allowed to call.
This is polymorphism, meaning one call results in many behaviors.
concepts.source_ref: Lecture 14: Inheritance and polymorphism in Java · Dynamic dispatch.

key_points: Inheritance lets a subclass reuse and specialize a superclass using extends.
The subclass inherits public and protected members.
Constructors are not inherited and the subclass constructor must call super(...) first.
concepts.source_ref: Lecture 14: Inheritance and polymorphism in Java · Lecture 14: Inheritance and polymorphism

key_points: Overriding involves the same name and parameters in a subclass, resolved at run time.
Overloading involves the same name with different parameter lists in the same class, resolved at compile time.
Use @Override so the compiler checks your overriding methods.
concepts.source_ref: Lecture 14: Inheritance and polymorphism in Java · Overriding vs. overloading.

key_points: Abstract classes cannot be instantiated and subclasses must implement their abstract methods.
Use an abstract class when subclasses share state or code.
Use an interface when you only need a contract.
concepts.source_ref: Lecture 14: Inheritance and polymorphism in Java · Abstract classes.

key_points: Prefer composition when the relationship is not truly an is-a relationship.
Inheriting from a class like ArrayList can expose unwanted methods.
A course has a list of students rather than being a kind of ArrayList.
concepts.source_ref: Lecture 14: Inheritance and polymorphism in Java · When not to inherit.

key_points: Write a failing test first, write the minimum code to pass, and then refactor.
Follow the cycle known as Red, green, refactor.
Forces you to decide what the code should do before deciding how to implement it.
concepts.source_ref: Lecture 16: JUnit and test-driven development · Test-driven development

key_points: Follow the three steps: arrange (build objects), act (call the method), and assert (check the result).
Test only one behavior per test.
Use a descriptive name that clearly states what the test checks, such as testConstructorRejectsNullName.
concepts.source_ref: Lecture 16: JUnit and test-driven development · Anatomy of a test

key_points: Use assertThrows to verify that a specific exception is thrown.
Check both the exception type and the specific error message returned.
Avoid catching exceptions and failing silently, which is a common mistake.
concepts.source_ref: Lecture 16: JUnit and test-driven development · Testing exceptions

key_points: Tests must not depend on execution order or on each other.
Use @BeforeEach to rebuild fixtures for every test.
Avoid sharing mutable state between tests to ensure independence.
concepts.source_ref: Lecture 16: JUnit and test-driven development · Test independence

key_points: Throwable splits into Error and Exception.
Checked exceptions must be declared with throws or handled.
Unchecked exceptions extend RuntimeException and signal programmer errors.
concepts.source_ref: Lecture 18: Exceptions and finite state machines · Exceptions

key_points: The finally block always runs, even after a return or an uncaught exception.
Catch specific exceptions before general ones.
Never leave a catch block empty.
concepts.source_ref: Lecture 18: Exceptions and finite state machines · try, catch, finally

key_points: Public class ConflictException extends Exception.
Includes two constructors: one with a message and one with a default message.
Throw it when adding an activity that overlaps an existing one.
concepts.source_ref: Lecture 18: Exceptions and finite state machines · Custom exceptions

key_points: A state machine has a finite set of states, an initial state, and transitions triggered by inputs.
Draw it as a diagram before coding where each arrow is one transition.
Testing requires one test per transition plus tests for invalid inputs.
concepts.source_ref: Lecture 18: Exceptions and finite state machines · Finite state machines

key_points: The context class holds a reference to its current State object and delegates actions.
Concrete states implement the transitions that make sense for them.
Benefits include avoiding giant switch statements and easily adding new states.
concepts.source_ref: Lecture 18: Exceptions and finite state machines · The State pattern

key_points: Activity is an abstract class containing title, meeting days, start time, and end time.
Course extends Activity and adds name, section, credits, and instructor id.
WolfScheduler manages the course catalog and the student schedule.
concepts.source_ref: Project 1 requirements: WolfScheduler · Required classes.

key_points: Course names must match a department code of 1 to 4 letters, a space, and 3 digits.
Credits must be a value between 1 and 5.
Any invalid value must throw an IllegalArgumentException with the exact message from requirements.
concepts.source_ref: Project 1 requirements: WolfScheduler · Rules to enforce.

key_points: Two activities conflict if they share at least one meeting day and their times overlap.
Sharing a single minute constitutes a time overlap.
Adding a conflicting activity to the schedule throws a ConflictException.
concepts.source_ref: Project 1 requirements: WolfScheduler · Conflicts.

key_points: A tax drives a wedge between the price buyers pay and the price sellers receive.
The outcome is identical whether the tax is collected from buyers or sellers.
The burden of the tax falls more heavily on the side of the market that is less elastic.
concepts.source_ref: Lecture 11: Taxes and deadweight loss · Lecture 11: Taxes and deadweight loss

key_points: Tax revenue equals the tax per unit multiplied by the quantity sold with the tax.
On a graph, tax revenue is represented as a rectangle.
concepts.source_ref: Lecture 11: Taxes and deadweight loss · Lecture 11: Taxes and deadweight loss

key_points: Deadweight loss occurs because beneficial trades between the old and new quantities no longer happen.
It is represented graphically as the triangle between the demand and supply curves over the lost range.
Deadweight loss is calculated as one-half times the tax times the fall in quantity.
concepts.source_ref: Lecture 11: Taxes and deadweight loss · Lecture 11: Taxes and deadweight loss

key_points: The more elastic demand or supply is, the larger the fall in quantity and the bigger the deadweight loss.
Doubling a tax roughly quadruples the deadweight loss because the triangle scales with the square of the tax.
Tax revenue initially rises with higher taxes, but eventually falls at very high taxes, forming the Laffer curve.
concepts.source_ref: Lecture 11: Taxes and deadweight loss · Lecture 11: Taxes and deadweight loss

key_points: Measures how much quantity demanded responds to a price change.
Calculated as the percentage change in quantity divided by the percentage change in price and reported as a positive number.
Classified as elastic if greater than 1, inelastic if less than 1, and unit elastic if exactly 1.
concepts.source_ref: Lecture 6: Elasticity · Lecture 6: Elasticity (chapter 5)

key_points: Uses the average of the two prices and the two quantities as the base.
Ensures the calculated elasticity is the same regardless of the direction of movement.
Formula divides percentage change in quantity by percentage change in price using these averages.
concepts.source_ref: Lecture 6: Elasticity · Midpoint method.

key_points: Demand is more elastic when close substitutes are available.
Luxuries have more elastic demand than necessities, and narrowly defined markets are more elastic than broadly defined ones.
A longer time horizon makes demand more elastic because people find alternatives eventually.
concepts.source_ref: Lecture 6: Elasticity · What makes demand more elastic:

key_points: Total revenue is calculated as price times quantity.
If demand is inelastic, a price rise increases total revenue because quantity falls proportionally less.
If demand is elastic, a price rise lowers total revenue.
concepts.source_ref: Lecture 6: Elasticity · Total revenue test.

key_points: Income elasticity is positive for normal goods and negative for inferior goods.
Cross-price elasticity is positive for substitutes and negative for complements.
Price elasticity of supply measures how quantity supplied responds to price and is higher when producers can adjust easily.
concepts.source_ref: Lecture 6: Elasticity · Other elasticities.

key_points: Willingness to pay is the maximum amount a buyer would pay.
Consumer surplus is willingness to pay minus the price actually paid, summed over all buyers.
It is represented graphically as the area below the demand curve and above the price.
When the price falls, existing buyers gain and new buyers enter to add to consumer surplus.
concepts.source_ref: Lecture 9: Consumer and producer surplus · Lecture 9

key_points: Cost is the minimum a seller would accept, representing the opportunity cost of producing.
Producer surplus is the price received minus the cost, summed over all sellers.
It is represented graphically as the area above the supply curve and below the price.
concepts.source_ref: Lecture 9: Consumer and producer surplus · Lecture 9

key_points: Total surplus is the sum of consumer surplus and producer surplus, equal to value to buyers minus cost to sellers.
The free-market equilibrium maximizes total surplus.
Goods go to buyers who value them most and are produced by sellers with the lowest cost.
Producing less than equilibrium leaves valuable trades unmade, while producing more means units cost more than they are worth.
concepts.source_ref: Lecture 9: Consumer and producer surplus · Lecture 9

key_points: Efficiency is not equity, meaning the market says nothing about whether the income distribution is fair.
The efficiency result assumes perfectly competitive markets with no externalities.
When these assumptions fail, the market no longer maximizes surplus.
concepts.source_ref: Lecture 9: Consumer and producer surplus · Lecture 9

key_points: Any linear two-terminal circuit is equivalent to a single voltage source Vth in series with Rth
It is also equivalent to a current source In in parallel with Rth
In equals Vth divided by Rth
concepts.source_ref: Lecture 10: Thevenin and Norton equivalents · Lecture 10: Thevenin and Norton equivalents

key_points: Vth is the open-circuit voltage across the terminals with the load removed
In is the short-circuit current with the terminals shorted
Rth with independent sources is found by turning off every source and computing the resistance seen from the terminals
concepts.source_ref: Lecture 10: Thevenin and Norton equivalents · Finding Vth

key_points: A load receives maximum power when RL equals Rth
The maximum power received is Vth squared divided by four Rth
Efficiency is only 50 percent at maximum power transfer because half the power is lost in Rth
concepts.source_ref: Lecture 10: Thevenin and Norton equivalents · Maximum power transfer

key_points: A voltage source Vs in series with R is interchangeable with a current source Vs over R in parallel with R
This is useful for simplifying a circuit step by step before applying node analysis
concepts.source_ref: Lecture 10: Thevenin and Norton equivalents · Source transformation

key_points: The current-voltage relationship is i = C dv/dt.
Voltage across a capacitor cannot change instantly because that would require infinite current.
At DC steady state a capacitor acts as an open circuit.
Energy stored in a capacitor is (1/2) C v^2.
concepts.source_ref: Lecture 12: RC circuits and time constants · Capacitor basics

key_points: A capacitor charged to V0 connected across a resistor discharges according to v(t) = V0 e^(-t/tau).
The time constant is defined as tau = RC.
After one time constant the voltage is 37% of V0, and after five time constants it is under 1%.
concepts.source_ref: Lecture 12: RC circuits and time constants · Discharging

key_points: The general formula for any RC or RL circuit is x(t) = x_final + (x_initial - x_final) e^(-t/tau).
You must find the initial value just after the switch, where capacitor voltage is continuous.
You must find the final value, treating the capacitor as an open circuit.
The time constant is calculated as tau = R_th C using the Thevenin resistance seen by the capacitor.
concepts.source_ref: Lecture 12: RC circuits and time constants · Charging

key_points: Inductors are the dual of capacitors with the relationship v = L di/dt.
Current through an inductor cannot change instantly.
At DC steady state an inductor acts as a short circuit.
The time constant for an inductor circuit is tau = L / R_th and stored energy is (1/2) L i^2.
concepts.source_ref: Lecture 12: RC circuits and time constants · Inductors are the dual

key_points: Pick one node as the reference ground at 0 V.
Label the remaining unknown node voltages.
Write Kirchhoff's current law at each non-reference node.
Solve the resulting linear equations.
concepts.source_ref: Lecture 8: Node voltage analysis · Procedure

key_points: A voltage source between a node and ground fixes that node's voltage and removes one unknown.
A voltage source between two non-reference nodes forms a supernode.
Write one KCL equation for the supernode pair plus the constraint equation.
concepts.source_ref: Lecture 8: Node voltage analysis · Voltage sources

key_points: Write the controlling quantity in terms of node voltages first.
Substitute the controlling quantity into the equations.
The resulting equations remain linear.
concepts.source_ref: Lecture 8: Node voltage analysis · Dependent sources

key_points: Current through each resistor should satisfy Ohm's law using the solved voltages.
Currents at every node should sum to zero.
Power delivered by sources must equal power absorbed by resistors.
concepts.source_ref: Lecture 8: Node voltage analysis · Checks

key_points: No current flows into the input terminals.
With negative feedback, the two input voltages are equal.
Everything in this lab follows from these two rules plus KCL at the inverting input.
concepts.source_ref: Lab 5 handout: Op-amp amplifiers · Ideal op-amp rules

key_points: Input goes through R1 to the inverting terminal with Rf from output to inverting terminal.
The non-inverting terminal is grounded.
Gain is calculated as -Rf / R1.
concepts.source_ref: Lab 5 handout: Op-amp amplifiers · Inverting amplifier

key_points: Input goes directly to the non-inverting terminal.
Gain is calculated as 1 + Rf / R1.
Input resistance is very high, making this preferred for weak sources.
concepts.source_ref: Lab 5 handout: Op-amp amplifiers · Non-inverting amplifier

key_points: The output cannot exceed the supply rails.
With plus or minus 15 V supplies, the rails are about plus or minus 13.5 V.
Increasing input amplitude causes the output to clip flat.
concepts.source_ref: Lab 5 handout: Op-amp amplifiers · Saturation

concepts.topic: Node Voltage and Mesh Current Analysis
key_points: Includes supernodes and dependent sources.
Partial credit is given for a correct setup including a chosen and labeled reference node.
KCL equations must be written correctly for partial credit even if algebra fails.
concepts.source_ref: Midterm review sheet · Coverage and Format

key_points: Covers Thevenin and Norton equivalents.
Includes source transformation and superposition.
Applies the maximum power transfer formula.
concepts.source_ref: Midterm review sheet · Coverage

key_points: Uses the universal first-order solution equation.
Time constant tau is calculated as RC for RC circuits and L/R for RL circuits.
Involves capacitors and inductors.
concepts.source_ref: Midterm review sheet · Coverage and Provided

concepts.topic: Integration by Parts Formula and Choosing u
key_points: The formula is derived from the product rule as integral of u dv = u v - integral of v du
Choose u as the factor that gets simpler when differentiated
Use the LIATE priority list where earlier items make better choices for u
concepts.source_ref: Lecture 10: Integration by parts · Lecture 10: Integration by parts (section 7.1)

key_points: Some integrals require applying parts twice, such as x^2 sin x
The tabular method uses alternating signs with derivatives in one column and integrals in the other
Sign mistakes in the second round are the most common error
concepts.source_ref: Lecture 10: Integration by parts · Integrals that need parts twice

key_points: Applying parts twice to e^x cos x makes the original integral reappear on the right side
Move the recurring integral to the left side and divide by 2
The same trick can be used for e^x sin x and sec^3 x
concepts.source_ref: Lecture 10: Integration by parts · Integrals that return to themselves

key_points: The integral of ln x uses u = ln x and dv = dx
The integral of arctan x results in x arctan x - (1/2) ln(1 + x^2) + C
concepts.source_ref: Lecture 10: Integration by parts · Sneaky single-factor cases

key_points: Use x = a sin t for sqrt(a^2 - x^2), x = a tan t for sqrt(a^2 + x^2), and x = a sec t for sqrt(x^2 - a^2).
The root collapses using standard trig identities like 1 - sin^2 = cos^2.
Draw a right triangle at the end to convert the trig functions back to the variable x.
concepts.source_ref: Lecture 13: Trig substitution and partial fractions · Lecture 13: Trigonometric substitution and partial fractions (sections 7.3-7.4)

key_points: Decompose a proper rational function P(x)/Q(x) where the degree of P is less than the degree of Q.
Factor the denominator Q completely into linear and irreducible quadratic factors.
Assign terms like A / (x - a) for distinct linear factors and (Ax + B) / (x^2 + bx + c) for irreducible quadratics.
concepts.source_ref: Lecture 13: Trig substitution and partial fractions · Lecture 13: Trigonometric substitution and partial fractions (sections 7.3-7.4)

key_points: Multiply through by the common denominator Q(x).
Plug in the roots to find constants quickly using the cover-up method for distinct linear factors.
Alternatively, match coefficients of powers of x to solve for the unknown constants.
concepts.source_ref: Lecture 13: Trig substitution and partial fractions · Lecture 13: Trigonometric substitution and partial fractions (sections 7.3-7.4)

key_points: Defined as the limit of a definite integral as the upper limit goes to infinity.
The integral converges if the limit exists and is finite, and diverges otherwise.
The integral of 1/x^p converges exactly when p > 1.
concepts.source_ref: Lecture 16: Improper integrals · Type 1: infinite interval

key_points: Occurs when f blows up at an endpoint, requiring a one-sided limit.
The integral of 1/x^p converges exactly when p < 1, which is the opposite of type 1.
A discontinuity in the middle of the interval must be split into two integrals, and both must converge.
concepts.source_ref: Lecture 16: Improper integrals · Type 2: infinite discontinuity

key_points: Failing to check for discontinuities inside the interval leads to incorrect results like negative values.
Always check for discontinuities inside the interval before integrating.
concepts.source_ref: Lecture 16: Improper integrals · Common trap

key_points: If 0 <= f(x) <= g(x) and the integral of g converges, the integral of f also converges.
If the integral of f diverges, the integral of g also diverges.
Used when you cannot find an antiderivative.
concepts.source_ref: Lecture 16: Improper integrals · Comparison test

key_points: Use partial fractions to split the integrand into 1/x - 1/(x + 1).
Evaluate the antiderivative as ln(x / (x + 1)).
Take the limit as the upper bound goes to infinity to find the value ln 2.
concepts.source_ref: Quiz 3 solutions · Problem 1

key_points: Recognize that the integrand is undefined at x = 1 inside the interval from 0 to 2.
Split the integral at the point of discontinuity x = 1.
Show that the limit diverges to infinity, and avoid integrating straight through.
concepts.source_ref: Quiz 3 solutions · Problem 2

key_points: Use the bound 1 <= 2 + sin x <= 3 to bound the numerator.
Compare the integrand to 3/x^2.
Conclude convergence using the p-test with p = 2.
concepts.source_ref: Quiz 3 solutions · Problem 3

key_points: Write the limit before evaluating the integral.
State whether the integral converges or diverges.
Know the p-test for both types and the comparison test.
concepts.source_ref: Test 2 review: sequences and series · Improper integrals (7.8)

key_points: Arc length L is the integral of sqrt(1 + (dy/dx)^2) dx.
Set up and simplify under the root before integrating so the root collapses.
Surface area of revolution S about the x-axis is the integral of 2 pi y sqrt(1 + (dy/dx)^2) dx.
concepts.source_ref: Test 2 review: sequences and series · Arc length (8.1)

key_points: A sequence converges if the limit of a_n exists.
Use L'Hopital on the related function, the squeeze theorem, and the fact that r^n goes to 0 when |r| < 1.
A bounded monotonic sequence converges.
concepts.source_ref: Test 2 review: sequences and series · Sequences (11.1)

key_points: A series converges if its partial sums converge.
Geometric series sum of a r^n converges to a / (1 - r) when |r| < 1 and diverges otherwise.
If a_n does not go to 0, the divergence test shows the series diverges.
concepts.source_ref: Test 2 review: sequences and series · Series (11.2)

key_points: For positive, continuous, decreasing terms, the series and the integral converge or diverge together.
A p-series of the sum of 1/n^p converges exactly when p > 1.
The limit comparison test states that if a_n / b_n has a positive finite limit, both series behave the same way.
concepts.source_ref: Test 2 review: sequences and series · Integral test (11.3)

key_points: First law: an object with zero net force moves at constant velocity or stays at rest.
Second law: net force equals mass times acceleration, applied one axis at a time.
Third law: forces come in equal and opposite pairs acting on different objects.
concepts.source_ref: Lecture 11: Newton's laws and free-body diagrams · Lecture 11: Newton's laws and free-body diagrams

key_points: Isolate one object and draw every real force acting on it.
Do not draw ma or velocity as forces.
Choose axes, usually with one axis along the acceleration, and write the sum of forces for each axis.
concepts.source_ref: Lecture 11: Newton's laws and free-body diagrams · Free-body diagram procedure.

key_points: For a block on a frictionless incline, set axes along and perpendicular to the surface.
The component of weight down the slope drives the acceleration.
The normal force is less than mg.
concepts.source_ref: Lecture 11: Newton's laws and free-body diagrams · Incline example.

key_points: Draw separate diagrams for each object tied by a rope.
The tension has the same magnitude on both masses connected by a massless rope and frictionless pulley.
Add the equations of motion for both objects to solve for acceleration and tension.
concepts.source_ref: Lecture 11: Newton's laws and free-body diagrams · Connected objects.

key_points: In an elevator accelerating upward, the scale reads m(g + a).
In an elevator accelerating downward, the scale reads m(g - a).
Apparent weight is zero in free fall.
concepts.source_ref: Lecture 11: Newton's laws and free-body diagrams · Apparent weight.

concepts.topic: Work done by a constant force
key_points: Calculated using W = F d cos(theta) where theta is the angle between the force and displacement.
Work is a scalar measured in joules.
A force perpendicular to the motion does no work while a force opposing motion does negative work.
concepts.source_ref: Lecture 14: Work and kinetic energy · Lecture 14: Work and kinetic energy (chapter 9)

concepts.topic: Kinetic energy and the work-energy theorem
key_points: Kinetic energy is defined as K = (1/2) m v^2.
The net work done on an object equals its change in kinetic energy.
It provides the fastest route to a speed when the path is messy but forces are known.
concepts.source_ref: Lecture 14: Work and kinetic energy · Lecture 14: Work and kinetic energy (chapter 9)

key_points: Work by a variable force is the integral of F(x) dx or the area under the force-position graph.
For a spring where F = -k x, the work done by the spring from x1 to x2 is (1/2) k x1^2 - (1/2) k x2^2.
Stretching a spring from rest to x requires (1/2) k x^2 of work by you.
concepts.source_ref: Lecture 14: Work and kinetic energy · Lecture 14: Work and kinetic energy (chapter 9)

key_points: Power is the rate of doing work expressed as P = W / t.
It can also be calculated as P = F v for a force along the velocity.
Power is measured in units of watts.
concepts.source_ref: Lecture 14: Work and kinetic energy · Lecture 14: Work and kinetic energy (chapter 9)

key_points: Mean is calculated as the sum of x over n.
Variance uses n minus 1 in the denominator.
Outliers are defined as values below Q1 minus 1.5 IQR or above Q3 plus 1.5 IQR.
concepts.source_ref: Midterm formula sheet · Descriptive statistics

key_points: The addition rule is P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A and B).
The multiplication rule for independent events is P(A and B) = P(A) P(B).
Conditional probability is calculated as P(A and B) divided by P(B).
concepts.source_ref: Midterm formula sheet · Probability

key_points: Expected value is the sum of x times P(x).
Binomial mean is n p and standard deviation is the square root of n p (1 - p).
concepts.source_ref: Midterm formula sheet · Random variables

key_points: The formula is x-bar plus or minus t* times s over the square root of n.
Degrees of freedom is n minus 1.
concepts.source_ref: Midterm formula sheet · Confidence interval for a mean

key_points: Replacing the population standard deviation with the sample standard deviation adds uncertainty.
The t-distribution is bell-shaped but has heavier tails than the normal distribution.
As degrees of freedom increase, the t-distribution approaches the normal distribution.
concepts.source_ref: Lecture 11: Confidence intervals for a mean · Why t instead of z

concepts.topic: Conditions for a Mean Confidence Interval
key_points: Requires a random sample or a reasonable argument for representativeness.
Requires independence, meaning the sample must be under 10% of the population.
Requires normality, meaning the population is roughly normal or the sample size is at least 30 without extreme outliers.
concepts.source_ref: Lecture 11: Confidence intervals for a mean · Conditions

key_points: A 95% confidence interval means the method captures the true mean in 95% of samples.
It does not mean there is a 95% probability that the mean lies within a specific calculated interval.
The interval says nothing about individual observations.
concepts.source_ref: Lecture 11: Confidence intervals for a mean · Interpretation

key_points: The margin of error shrinks with a larger sample size by the square root of n.
To halve the margin of error, the sample size must be quadrupled.
Increasing the confidence level from 95% to 99% makes the interval wider.
concepts.source_ref: Lecture 11: Confidence intervals for a mean · Margin of error

key_points: A statistic like the sample mean changes from sample to sample.
The sampling distribution is the distribution of a statistic over all possible samples of size n.
It helps determine how far a sample mean is likely to be from the population mean.
concepts.source_ref: Lecture 7: Sampling distributions and the Central Limit Theorem · Lecture 7: Sampling distributions and the Central Limit Theorem

key_points: The mean of the sampling distribution of the sample mean equals the population mean.
The standard error is the standard deviation of the sample mean, calculated as sigma divided by the square root of n.
Larger sample sizes produce less variable sample means, where quadrupling the sample size halves the standard error.
concepts.source_ref: Lecture 7: Sampling distributions and the Central Limit Theorem · Facts about the sample mean

key_points: For a large enough sample, the sampling distribution of the sample mean is approximately normal.
This approximation holds regardless of the shape of the population distribution.
If the population is already normal, the sample mean is exactly normal for any sample size.
Skewed populations require larger sample sizes to achieve normality.
concepts.source_ref: Lecture 7: Sampling distributions and the Central Limit Theorem · Central Limit Theorem

key_points: Confidence intervals and tests for a mean rely on the normal or t shape guaranteed by the CLT.
These statistical methods are not trustworthy when the sample size is small and the population is not normal.
Simulations show that histograms of sample means become narrower and more bell-shaped as sample size increases, even if a single sample remains skewed.
concepts.source_ref: Lecture 7: Sampling distributions and the Central Limit Theorem · Why it matters

key_points: Assumes that the two populations have the same variance.
Uses a pooled variance formula with n1+n2-2 degrees of freedom.
Recommended when sample standard deviations are within a factor of about 2 of each other.
concepts.source_ref: Lecture 9: Two-sample t tests (pooled vs. Welch) · Pooled t test

key_points: Does not assume equal variances between the two populations.
Degrees of freedom are computed using the Welch-Satterthwaite formula and are usually not a whole number.
It is the default test in R's t.test() and loses very little power when variances are actually equal.
concepts.source_ref: Lecture 9: Two-sample t tests (pooled vs. Welch) · Welch t test

key_points: Requires independent random samples.
Requires either normal populations or sample sizes large enough for the CLT (about 30 each).
Boxplots should be used to check the data for strong skew and outliers.
concepts.source_ref: Lecture 9: Two-sample t tests (pooled vs. Welch) · Conditions for both

key_points: Using var.equal = TRUE in t.test() runs the pooled test, while omitting it runs the Welch test.
Important values to report include the t statistic, degrees of freedom, p-value, and confidence interval.
The confidence interval is highly important because it shows how big the difference plausibly is.
concepts.source_ref: Lecture 9: Two-sample t tests (pooled vs. Welch) · Reading R output

key_points: Use histograms, boxplots, and QQ plots to check the data before running tests.
Points near the line on the QQ plot suggest approximate normality.
Mild skew is fine with n above 30 per group.
concepts.source_ref: R Lab 3 handout: t.test() and checking assumptions · Step 1, look before testing

key_points: Test if the mean sleep is different from 7 hours using t.test(d$hours, mu = 7).
Read off the t statistic, degrees of freedom, p-value, and 95% confidence interval.
concepts.source_ref: R Lab 3 handout: t.test() and checking assumptions · Step 2, one-sample test

key_points: Run t.test(hours ~ group, data = d) which uses Welch by default.
Add var.equal = TRUE to run the pooled test.
Comparing the two outputs shows differing degrees of freedom with usually agreeing conclusions.
concepts.source_ref: R Lab 3 handout: t.test() and checking assumptions · Step 3, two-sample test

key_points: The confidence interval for the difference in means is the most useful number to report.
A proper write-up is two or three sentences covering what was compared, the test used, the estimate with its interval, and the plain conclusion.
concepts.source_ref: R Lab 3 handout: t.test() and checking assumptions · Step 4 and Step 5
